claim: The Plus Beaux Villages de Wallonie network officially recognises 33 labelled villages across Wallonia, including Celles, Crupet, Falaën, Mozet, Sosoye, Soulme and Thon-Samson in Namur province.
quote: the association Les Plus Beaux Villages de Wallonie oversees a network of 33 villages, all of which bear a strong territorial identity and reflect traditional architecture

claim: Sosoye sits along meanders of the Molignée with limestone Condroz houses, an 18th-century Nativity church, listed presbytery and 17th-century tithe barn, near Maredsous Abbey.
quote: meanders of the picturesque Molignée with limestone houses typical of the Condroz valley along its main street, surrounded by the steep inclines of the Ranzinelle Mountain

claim: Thon-Samson overlooks the Meuse and Samson valleys and features the 18th-century Forge Castle, ruins of the Samson Fortress on a rocky promontory, and the Scladina prehistoric grotto.
quote: Forge Castle (18th c.), an impressive classical residence with a tower of medieval inspiration, and the ruins of the Samson Fortress standing on a rocky promontory above the confluence of the Samson and Meuse rivers

claim: Mozet is a Namur-province Plus Beaux Villages member with traditional stone architecture set in the Samson valley.

Crupet's Grotte Saint-Antoine de Padoue, an artificial grotto built 1900–1903 by villagers under Canon Jules Gérard, stages life-of-the-saint scenes; its devil tableau is the most famous, with free parking and views of the keep behind the Pachis café.
quote: The artificial caves were built between 1900 and 1903 by the inhabitants of the village at the instigation of Canon Jules Gérard... The devil scene, which is very impressive, is the most famous.

claim: Crupet's 13th-century Carondelet keep, converted into a castle-farm in the 16th century and listed since 1973, was restored through 2020; the village has a 2 km interpretation trail and thirteen marked walks of 4–13 km.
quote: The Carondelet keep is a must-see... a 13th-century fortified tower that was converted into a castle-farm in the 16th century... underwent significant renovation work until 2020

claim: Celles, in the Houyet commune of Namur Condroz, is anchored by the 11th-century Collégiale Saint-Hadelin, considered the most perfect expression of Mosan Romanesque art and classified Exceptional Heritage of Wallonia.
quote: Celles, village chef d'œuvre d'art Roman

claim: Falaën in the Molignée valley pairs with the romantic ruins of Montaigle castle (destroyed 1554 by Henry II's troops), with the famous Molignée draisine railbike running from the foot of the castle to the old Maredsous station.
quote: Standing on an abrupt, rocky spur overlooking the pretty Molignée valley, the Montaigle site is one of the loveliest examples of the medieval castle so dear to the Romantics

claim: Soulme, perched above the Hermeton valley with Fagne-style architecture, features the listed 11th-century St. Columba church, a 17th/18th-century mill and the former monks' farm, and is a launchpad for rural walks.
quote: Perched at the summit of its hilltop overlooking the Hermeton valley, Soulme features typical Fagne architecture nestled in a verdant setting

claim: The Maison du Patrimoine Médiéval Mosan in Bouvignes-sur-Meuse (Place du Bailliage 16, 5500 Dinant) opens Tue–Sun 10:00–18:00 (April–October) or 10:00–17:00 (November–March); adults €8, audioguides in FR/NL/EN, typical visit 1.5 h.
quote: From April 1 to October 31: Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00 AM to 6:00 PM. From November 1 to March 31: Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00 AM to 5:00 PM

claim: Dinant's Charles de Gaulle bridge is decorated since 2010 with 28 oversized painted saxophones, each placed before a national flag honouring a member country, paying tribute to Adolphe Sax (born Dinant 1814, saxophone patented 1846).
quote: Installed in 2010, 28 saxophones adorn the Charles de Gaulle bridge. Painted in unique colors, one saxophone takes on the appearance of a basketball, another looks like a mermaid

claim: Namur's Halle al'Chair, a late-16th-century Mosan-Renaissance red-brick-and-stone hall built 1588–1590 by Bastien Sion and Conrad de Nuremberg as a butchers' market, today houses the Namur Tourist Office at the foot of the Citadel.
quote: The Halle al'Chair is an architectural marvel by the Sambre River, originally a butcher's hub from 1588 to 1590, and it now houses the Namur Tourist Office

claim: Namur's old-town rue de Fer is the city's main shopping street running off Place de l'Ange, and the nearby Baroque Saint-Loup church (17th c.) is considered one of Belgium's most beautiful Baroque interiors.
quote: Rue de Fer is also where you'll find public toilets and the City Hall... The Saint-Loup Catholic Church, a 17th-century church and one of the most beautiful Baroque buildings in Belgium

claim: Wépion is Belgium's strawberry capital; the Musée de la Fraise hosts exhibits on history and cultivation plus a berry garden with 15 strawberry varieties, with English translations and a gift shop of strawberry liqueurs and jams.
quote: the village of Wépion, and teaches visitors all about the tasty fruit... The museum also boasts a berry garden with 15 varieties of strawberries

claim: The Rochers de Frênes belvedere on the Lustin/Profondeville bank towers roughly 100 m above the Meuse, with limestone cliffs once 800 m high before river erosion, offering the iconic Meuse panorama opposite Profondeville church.
quote: The rocks are an impressive peak about 100 meters above the Meuse, with limestone formations that culminated at 800 meters millions of years ago before being eroded by the Meuse river

claim: The Promenade des 7 Meuses is a 7.3–7.5 km loop between Lustin and Godinne stations (~2 h 30, 170 m climb) combining forest and Ravel sections that reaches a viewpoint over seven Meuse meanders, also used by paragliders.
quote: At the famous Les Sept Meuses viewpoint, you can see seven meanders of the Meuse, and on clear days the view extends to the French border

claim: Profondeville's seasonal Belle de Frênes passage d'eau rows visitors across the Meuse opposite the Rochers de Frênes massif, giving water-level views of the cliffs.
